On 9/30/13 6:41 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I would be happy to answer specific questions.

Thanks.

> I think the names are fine.  I always find it hard to give names and you
> cannot extrapolate much from them.

I just wrote a section on why naming is important for
the Stan 2.0 manual :-)  But like doc, they can be
misleading.  (Like the user who was using "prec" for
a covariance matrix.)

> And it might be better not to look at rstan for implementing pystan.  Directly taking a look at stan would be better as
> rstan is mimicking stan (specifically command.hpp).

Having a look at implementations can be really helpful!

> Practically, I was just trying to make it work given R and Rcpp's
> functionality.

It's pretty much impossible to see into the future.  The best we
can do is continually improve the code as we understand it better.

At least that was the spirit in which I sent the previous few
e-mails.  We just went through a HUGE refactor on Stan itself.
And there are still a bunch of things that aren't quite organized
right yet.  Maybe by 3.0 ...

- Bob

I ran 2.0 command-line and saw the init value being

Nobody has any objections to saving the init point in the
output, do they?

gets numbered.  That is, if we count it as an iteration,
we get one less iteration than we did before.  If we
don't count it, then we get one too many lines in the CSV
file.

messages.subject: Re: variational inference via stan autodifferentiation
messages.body_plain:
On 10/4/13 5:40 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Perhaps we can discuss at the next Stan meeting.
>
> Definitely.

Sounds like fun.

>> I remain curious why we can't try implementing the full auto VB (the version that does not involve dividing the parameters into 2 sets).
>
> The idea is to make this scalable to the canonical "big data" problems were data can only be streamed and not held in memory all at once.

I'd think we'd want two versions of this for Stan.
One "batch" and one "stochastic".

>> Also, if we are dividing the parameters into 2 sets, it would be worth discussing more carefully the difference between your algorithm and my crude "lmer/glmer emulator" idea.
>
> Instead of optimizing the global parameters over the expectation of the local parameters we're hoping to find the variational distribution by taking all expectations.  It's just EM vs VB.

Won't stochastic VB give you the same answer as VB
(in principle, anyway)?

- Bob

On Sat, Oct 5, 2013 at 8:40 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Also, do you know how I can specify inits in RStan? I tried setting inits equal to a list of all of the initial values that I wanted to use:
>
>   radon_group_chr.sf1 <- sampling(radon_group_chr.sm <http://radon_group_chr.sm>, dataList.3, chains=1,init=dataList.4,sample_file=paste('radon_group_cp_',count,'.csv',sep=''))
>

>
> Error in config_argss(chains = chains, iter = iter, warmup = warmup, thin = thin,  :
>   initial value list mismatchs number of chains
> error specification of arguments; sampling not done

It needs to be a list, each element of which needs to be a list of all the initial values.  Suppose you have parameter alpha in your model, then the inits argument can be fed say for 4 chains as follows:

inits = list(c1=list(alpha=1), c2=list(alpha=2), c3=list(alpha=3), c4=list(alpha=4)).

So I think in your example, you should do init = list(dataList.4).

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: optimization in Stan 2?
messages.body_plain:
I'm stuck on doc for optimization because I can't make
it work reliably (I had no problem with Stan 1.3's).

Things I found confusing:

1.  I didn't get any output from the default.  The only
way I get output is if I set "save_iterations=1".  But I
somehow don't think this is right because I don't get any
output with "algorithm=newton" at all, even with save_iterations=1.
And in other configs of BFGS, I didn't get reasonable output, making
me think it was an intermediate iteration.

2.  When I ran, it said it was using BFGS, and

     ------------------------------
     /temp2/norm$ ./norm-fit optimize save_iterations=1
     ...
     initial log joint probability = -9.80884
         Iter      log prob        ||dx||      ||grad||       alpha      alpha0  # evals  Notes
            1     -0.525525       1.36259   9.31988e-11         0.1           1        3
     Optimization terminated with code 2
     ------------------------------------

     a.  What is code 2?   And whatever it is, we should make these
     return results a little more user friendly --- I thought I just
     had it misconfigured until I set save_iterations=1

     b.  What is code 1?  I got that in another situation when I had an
     init file.

     c.  What is that debug print?  It looks BFGS specific
       i.  Is ||grad|| just the L2 norm of the gradient?
      ii.  What is ||dx||?  Is that some kind of stepsize?
     iii.  What are alpha and alpha0?
     We can just make the output more verbose to make these more clear.

3.  Running with Newton has other problems.

     ----------------------
     ./norm-fit optimize algorithm=newton save_iterations=1
     initial log joint probability = 0
      Iteration  1. Log joint probability =  -0.525525. Improved by -0.525525.
     -------------------------

     a.  nothing written into output csv file other than config

     b.  no error message

4.  Do the empty paths in the output for files mean they're null?
     If so, some better print might help, and I can also add doc.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] optimization in Stan 2?
messages.body_plain:
On Sun, Oct 6, 2013 at 9:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I'm stuck on doc for optimization because I can't make
> it work reliably (I had no problem with Stan 1.3's).
>
> Things I found confusing:
>
> 1.  I didn't get any output from the default.  The only
> way I get output is if I set "save_iterations=1".  But I
> somehow don't think this is right because I don't get any
> output with "algorithm=newton" at all, even with save_iterations=1.
> And in other configs of BFGS, I didn't get reasonable output, making
> me think it was an intermediate iteration.

I believe the idea for the optimization algorithms was that it would only print a single point at the end unless save_iterations was specified but it's possible that this isn't happening.  I don't really test the save_iterations=0 path much at all in my typical usage because, well, convergence almost never happens.  I just don't have that kind of patience :)

>
> 2.  When I ran, it said it was using BFGS, and
>
>     ------------------------------
>     /temp2/norm$ ./norm-fit optimize save_iterations=1
>     ...
>     initial log joint probability = -9.80884
>         Iter      log prob        ||dx||      ||grad||       alpha      alpha0  # evals  Notes
>            1     -0.525525       1.36259   9.31988e-11         0.1           1        3
>     Optimization terminated with code 2
>     ------------------------------------
>
>     a.  What is code 2?   And whatever it is, we should make these
>     return results a little more user friendly --- I thought I just
>     had it misconfigured until I set save_iterations=1
>
>     b.  What is code 1?  I got that in another situation when I had an
>     init file.

Positive exit codes mean some kind of "normal" termination criteria.  In the above case, the norm of the gradient is small.  Exit code of zero means it hit the iteration limit.  Negative exit codes indicate termination for unusual reasons, typically indicating a badly behaved objective function.

>     c.  What is that debug print?  It looks BFGS specific

It is.

>       i.  Is ||grad|| just the L2 norm of the gradient?

Yes.

>      ii.  What is ||dx||?  Is that some kind of stepsize?

This is the size of the step that was taken at that iteration.  I.E., if x_i is the parameters at iteration i, dx = || x_i - x_{i-1} ||.

>     iii.  What are alpha and alpha0?

alpha is the step size taken by the line search.  alpha0 is the first value that's guessed based on heuristics.  Typically, with a well-behaved objective alpha = alpha0 = 1.

>     We can just make the output more verbose to make these more clear.

alpha0 could probably be removed.  It was put there while I was debugging some parts of the line search.  Now that things seem to be relatively stable, it doesn't provide much extra debugging information.

>
>
> 3.  Running with Newton has other problems.
>
>     ----------------------
>     ./norm-fit optimize algorithm=newton save_iterations=1
>     initial log joint probability = 0
>      Iteration  1. Log joint probability =  -0.525525. Improved by -0.525525.
>     -------------------------
>
>     a.  nothing written into output csv file other than config
>
>     b.  no error message
>
>
> 4.  Do the empty paths in the output for files mean they're null?
>     If so, some better print might help, and I can also add doc.

No idea on either of these, the Newton method hasn't seen much attention.  Personally, I'd like to see it removed until we can get autodiff'd Hessians.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Optimization broken in 2.0; "moving" to "experimental"
messages.body_plain:
I will work on fixing 1&2, they should be pretty easy.  I'd also like to expose more of the BFGS parameters to the user (convergence threshold, etc) if I can find the time.  Building a full suite of unit tests is beyond the time I have to give right now.  That said, some functional, high level tests wouldn't be hard to build.  For several models and functions we can implement the maxima are well known, e.g., the Rosenbrock function is one of the canonical test function for these kinds of optimization methods.

Anyway, it's fine by me to label optimization experimental, beta, whatever for now as most of it hasn't been widely tested.  I've personally never had much luck with the Nesterov optimizer and the Newton optimizer is going to be painfully slow for large models.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Is there a reason to have this function signature:

   real trace_quad_form(matrix m, vector v)

     =def=  trace(v' * m * v)

This looks like it'll define the same function as

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] bfgs parameters
messages.body_plain:
Just one of those conditions being satisfied will result in the algorithm terminating.

init_alpha has a default value (something like 0.0001) which is reasonable for many problems but might be too large or too small depending on the objective function and initialization.  Being too big or too small just means that the first iteration will take longer (require more gradient evaluations) before the line search finds a good step length.  It's not a critical parameter, but if you're optimizing the same model multiple times (as you tweak things or with different data) being able to change it can save some real time.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
What hath Xcode 5.0 wrought?

1.  I replicated the problem Jiqiang reported.  You can
solve it by increasing the template depth, as so:

is too shallow.)

   > make CC="clang++ -ftemplate-depth=512" O=0 bin/stanc'

took 10 minutes (nothing else running on my machine).

Most of that time was in a couple of grammars,
so I'm guessing it's related to the recursion issue.

I'm about to try O=3.  Wish me luck.

- Bob

messages.subject: Xcode 5's template-depth for g++/clang++ -- fix makefiles?
messages.subject_clean: Xcode 5's template-depth for g++/clang++ -- fix makefiles?
messages.body_plain:
The good news is that I forgot to run with -j4 the first time, so
it's only 5 minutes, not 10 minutes to build.  That's
still not good.

The default template depth of 128 in Xcode 5's version
of g++ and clang++ isn't enough.

Here's what gnu says:

   -ftemplate-depth=n
   Set the maximum instantiation depth for template classes to n. A limit
   on the template instantiation depth is needed
   to detect endless recursions during template class instantiation.
   ANSI/ISO C++ conforming programs must not rely on a
   maximum depth greater than 17 (changed to 1024 in C++11).
   The default value is 900, as the compiler can run out of
   stack space before hitting 1024 in some situations.

   http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/C_002b_002b-Dialect-Options.html

So we violate pre-C++11 but are OK with C++11.

Xcode for some reason used 128 as the default template-depth.  Ours isn't
the only project this broke when building in default settings.

I verified that we can build with:

   -ftemplate-depth=256

This works for both g++ and clang++, at least under Xcode 5.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob and/or Jiqiang,

On Thu, Oct 10, 2013 at 3:18 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> The good news is that I forgot to run with -j4 the first time, so
> it's only 5 minutes, not 10 minutes to build.  That's
> still not good.
>
> The default template depth of 128 in Xcode 5's version
> of g++ and clang++ isn't enough.
>
> Here's what gnu says:
>
>   -ftemplate-depth=n
>   Set the maximum instantiation depth for template classes to n. A limit
>   on the template instantiation depth is needed
>   to detect endless recursions during template class instantiation.
>   ANSI/ISO C++ conforming programs must not rely on a
>   maximum depth greater than 17 (changed to 1024 in C++11).
>   The default value is 900, as the compiler can run out of
>   stack space before hitting 1024 in some situations.
>
>   http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/C_002b_002b-Dialect-Options.html
>
> So we violate pre-C++11 but are OK with C++11.
>
> Xcode for some reason used 128 as the default template-depth.  Ours isn't
> the only project this broke when building in default settings.
>
> I verified that we can build with:
>
>   -ftemplate-depth=256
>
> This works for both g++ and clang++, at least under Xcode 5.

>
>
> - Bob

>     is released.
>
>     And we need to address the xcode 5 issue.

OPTION 1

The only fix for Xcode 5 is adding:

    -ftemplate-depth=256

to the call to g++ or clang++.  We need to get that fix
into Stan's makefile, too.

The problem is that Xcode now sets this to the tiny
value of 128, and that's not enough.  All the other compilers
have bigger depth limits and we need it for our code (I can't
figure out how to lower the depth required by the Spirit
parser framework down to 128).

OPTION 2

You can also get a more recent clang++ or g++ and
use those.  They'll compile faster and probably run
faster, too --- I haven't benchmarked the latest from
Xcode, though.

- Bob

> Just one of those conditions being satisfied will result in the algorithm terminating.
>
> init_alpha has a default value (something like 0.0001) which is reasonable for many problems but might be too large or too small depending on the objective function and initialization.  Being too big or too small just means that the first iteration will take longer (require more gradient evaluations) before the line search finds a good step length.  It's not a critical parameter, but if you're optimizing the same model multiple times (as you tweak things or with different data) being able to change it can save some real time.

messages.subject: python version numbering
messages.body_plain:
Looks like the Python convention is "c1" for what we're
calling RC1.

Reference below.

- Bob

From:  http://docs.python.org/2/faq/general.html#how-does-the-python-version-numbering-scheme-work

How does the Python version numbering scheme work?

Python versions are numbered A.B.C or A.B. A is the major version number ï¿½ it is only incremented for really major
changes in the language. B is the minor version number, incremented for less earth-shattering changes. C is the
micro-level ï¿½ it is incremented for each bugfix release. See PEP 6 for more information about bugfix releases.

Not all releases are bugfix releases. In the run-up to a new major release, a series of development releases are made,
denoted as alpha, beta, or release candidate. Alphas are early releases in which interfaces arenï¿½t yet finalized; itï¿½s
not unexpected to see an interface change between two alpha releases. Betas are more stable, preserving existing
interfaces but possibly adding new modules, and release candidates are frozen, making no changes except as needed to fix
critical bugs.

Alpha, beta and release candidate versions have an additional suffix. The suffix for an alpha version is ï¿½aNï¿½ for some
small number N, the suffix for a beta version is ï¿½bNï¿½ for some small number N, and the suffix for a release candidate
version is ï¿½cNï¿½ for some small number N. In other words, all versions labeled 2.0aN precede the versions labeled 2.0bN,
which precede versions labeled 2.0cN, and those precede 2.0.

You may also find version numbers with a ï¿½+ï¿½ suffix, e.g. ï¿½2.2+ï¿½. These are unreleased versions, built directly from the
Subversion trunk. In practice, after a final minor release is made, the Subversion trunk is incremented to the next
minor version, which becomes the ï¿½a0ï¿½ version, e.g. ï¿½2.4a0ï¿½.

See also the documentation for sys.version, sys.hexversion, and sys.version_info.

messages.subject: RStan memory leak?
messages.body_plain:
[moved to stan-dev from stan-users]

recover_memory() needs to be called after any evaluations
involving var objects.  You can see an example in
log_prob_propto() in:

   src/stan/model/util.hpp

You an also just call log_prob in the model with double
values, but that call doesn't drop all the constant terms,
so it gives you a different answer than log_prob_propto
as defined in util.

- Bob

> >   Set the maximum instantiation depth for template classes to n. A limit

> >   to detect endless recursions during template class instantiation.

> >
> > So we violate pre-C++11 but are OK with C++11.

The model log prob's defined for std::vector only.  The
refactoring never made it all the way through to the model.

The signature looks like this:

     template <bool propto__, bool jacobian__, typename T__>
     T__ log_prob(vector<T__>& params_r__,
                  vector<int>& params_i__,

                  std::ostream* pstream__ = 0) const;

And you shouldn't need the T in the call to log_prob in
the definition of operator() --- it should be inferrable from
the argument, which should be std::vector<T> --- but it
doesn't hurt to include it.

- Bob

>>         std::vector<int> dummy_int;
>>         return _model.log_prob<true,true,T>(eigen_x, dummy_int, _o);

>> src/stan/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/softabs_metric.hpp:28:41: error: expected ';' after return statement
>>         return _model.log_prob<true,true,T>(eigen_x, dummy_int, _o);

>>         fvar<var> fx_fvar = f(x_fvar);

>>>     std::ostream& o_;

>>>
>>> - Bob

messages.subject: Fwd: [stan-users] rstan wish: graceful failures
messages.body_plain:
Sometimes the init fails.  Should we save what's left?

I'm inclined to leave it how it is because an init failure
is a serious problem.

If we make this too easy, I worry that users are going to
remove chains that get stuck and make other changes with
subtle (or not-so-subtle) effects on detailed balance.

We got a request on the users list that I'd at least
like to reply to.

- Bob

Particularly when doing parallel calculations, failures cause problems
(I've also had failures because of insufficient RAM):

  > sflist <- mclapply(1:3, function(i) stan(fit=rb, data=stanDat, iter=8000, chains=1,
  +                                                      seed=seed, chain_id=i, refresh=-1,
  +                                                      warmup=500, thin=4),
  +                                mc.cores=3)
  Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or
reparameterizing the model.
  error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

  > a10 <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)
  Error in sflist2stanfit(sflist) :
    each 'stanfit' object in 'sflist' must contain samples

Wish #1: sflist2stanfit would combine all the valid runs. There may be
some subtleties in terms of the reported number of chains/iterations,
since using the original request isn't right.

Wish #2: make it easier to identify which objects have useable results.
My first thought was
> lapply(sflist, class)
[[1]]
[1] "stanfit"
attr(,"package")
[1] "rstan"

[[2]]
[1] "stanfit"
attr(,"package")
[1] "rstan"

[[3]]
[1] "stanfit"
attr(,"package")
[1] "rstan"

Nope, they all have the same class.

Reading the fine manual, I think the mode slot has the info I want.
> lapply(sflist, function(x) x@mode)
[[1]]
[1] 0

[[2]]
[1] 2

[[3]]
[1] 0

Wrapping that in an is.valid function (or some similar name) would be
helpful.

Ross Boylan

--

messages.body_plain:
I do not understand C++ one bit.

The class-functor:

    template <typename M>

    class _softabs_fun {

    public:

      _softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};

      template <typename T>

      T operator()(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {

        std::vector<T> v(x.size());

        Eigen::Map<Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1> >(&(v[0]), v.size()) = x;

        std::vector<int> dummy_int;

        return _model.log_prob<true,true,T>(v, dummy_int, _o);

      }

    private:

      const M& _model;

      std::ostream* _o;

    };

results in the errors:

src/stan/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/softabs_metric.hpp:30:41: error: expected ';' after return statement
        return _model.log_prob<true,true,T>(v, dummy_int, _o);
                                        ^
                                        ;
src/stan/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/softabs_metric.hpp:30:16: error: reference to non-static member function must be called
        return _model.log_prob<true,true,T>(v, dummy_int, _o);

I get that T in the log_prob instantiation can be inferred but I don't get why it errs out if I specify it explicitly.

Secondly, I have no idea why the compiler is can't reference the explicit model object.  Other model method work fine, it's just log_prob that errs.

Daniel and I were discussing how to organize the web pages.
With a beta release for 2 coming up and older versions, I
think we need a layer of indirection.

Something like a home page and then a per-product download page.
It's going to get too big with Python and then with MATLAB and maybe
even Stata.  And all the versioning is too busy for the home page.

So I'd suggest something like this, which I'd be happy to code up
today before the 2.0 release-candidate goes out.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
OK, as soon as I sat down to write this, I realized what the
problem was.  You need this:

template <typename M>
struct log_prob_functional {
   const M& m_;
   std::ostream& o_;
   log_prob_functional(const M& m, std::ostream& o)
     : m_(m), o_(o) {  }
   template <typename T>
   T operator()(const std::vector<T>& theta) {
     std::vector<int> ns;
     return m_.template log_prob<true,true,T>(theta,ns,o_);
   }
};

Note the absolutely absurd syntax "m_.template log_prob<true,true,T>".
C++ syntax is full of the need for these odd qualifications of what
seems obvious from looking at the expression, here that the function's
a template function!

- Bob

messages.subject: Windows tests & merging clean_up_fvar branch
messages.body_plain:
I believe the reason Peter's patches haven't been merged is
that the tests don't run under Windows --- it blows out stack
trying to compile the higher-order derivative code.

Of course, this means that we won't be able to run RMHMC
on Windows, either, but I'm OK with that.

I'd like to figure out how to merge in Peter's fixes,
though.   Can we conditionally not run some tests on Windows?

- Bob

It seems that the problem in the manual pointed out in the topic "min max for double" of the maling list is not solved yet.

> parameters {

(page 140 for tag 2.0.0)

should not use fmin(real) and fmax(real) since such signatures don't exist.

messages.subject: Refactoring the Stan repository
messages.body_plain:
Currently, the stan-dev/stan repository has multiple conceptual pieces inside it. Bob and I discussed this for a while yesterday and decided it would be good to split out the independent pieces.

This is how I'd like to split it apart:
stan-dev/stan: the core Stan library
C++ API
Stan reference manual
Most of the Stan compiler (stanc). The parts that live in src/stan/gm/ should stay.
stan-dev/cmdstan: the command line interface to Stan
CmdStan will be the command line / shell interface to Stan to mirror RStan and PyStan.
bin/print
bin/stanc
CmdStan will have its own getting started guide.
stan-dev/webpages: the webpages for mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>
stan-dev/example-models: Stan models and data
BUGS examples
ARM models
other models
possibly some descriptive text, maybe we can figure out how to put down stable values so each of the interfaces {R, Py, Cmd}Stan can test against the models

Some reasons for doing this:
CmdStan should be decoupled from the main Stan library.
{R, Py, Cmd}Stan can be released independently of upgrades to the Stan library.
Testing times can be reduced since there would be clear separation from unit tests and higher level tests.
Webpages can be uploaded independently without having to freeze and update Stan versions.
Makefiles can be simplified (I think).

If anyone has any thoughts, please send them out.

Daniel

On 10/18/13 12:22 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> How will CmdStan be refactored since it's currently implemented directly in the model executable?

I've been thinking for a while that it'd be nice to have
bin/stanc just compile the model and not the command.

I'd like to have the model compile w/o a main() in it.
It's not really part of the model concept, but rather
something that uses it.

If we make the model dynamically linkable, we can then compile
the command once and reuse it.

Otherwise, we can statically generate a new command with
the name of the model class in it and compile that and link
it to a .o for the model.

- Bob

messages.subject: debugging speed issue with 2.0
messages.body_plain:
Daniel just profiled the time of the log prob call in
2.0 vs. 1.3.  The log prob calls are a bit faster now
than they were in 2.0, so the problem's definitely in
the adaptation.

What I'm seeing is that if I stop adaptation after 100
iterations, the result's pretty similar to what we were
getting in 1.3.  But if I let 2.0 keep adaptating, then it
really bogs down.

Running through the Instruments profiler in Xcode didn't
show much difference in terms of where the time was being
spent, so I'm really confused about why the iterations are
so much slower in 2.0 than in 1.3.

- Bob

messages.subject: what to tell users about 2.0?
messages.body_plain:
Now that we've released 2.0.0, we see that there are models
that run MUCH MUCH more slowly in 2.0 than in 1.3.

What should we do at this point?  Daniel's been trying to track
down the "bug", but we don't know if it's even a bug or just
a "feature" that was introduced by reformulating adaptation and
varying step sizes as a mass matrix.

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Until this is fixed, my inclination is to put big red warning
labels on Stan 2.0 and tell users to only use it with caution.

I'm going to try to update the web site with links back to
how to install 1.3.  As is, we kind of erased tracks back to 1.3.
(Marcus warned us this would happen --- I didn't realize
that it would be so hard to find 1.3 once we reconfigured --- I
wasn't in the right user frame of mind.)

- Bob

You should be able to release RStan 2.0.1 at any point now.
That's one of the reasons we wanted to decouple Stan and RStan.

Whatever gets worked out on the Stan side for adaptation won't
affect the RStan interface.

Our hope is that any RStan with the same major and minor version (2.0
here) will work with any Stan version with matching major and minor
versions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] tree depth 0 vs. -1
messages.body_plain:
In theory, NUTS should always have at least a tree depth of 0, i.e. it should always accept at least one leapfrog step.  The issue is that NUTS is also defined on a slice, including only those points within a certain deltaH range (in particular, points outside of any constraints are not included).  -1 occurs when these two collide -- if the first step away form the initial point is not within the slice the initial point is returned.  If you really wanted to be pedantic, it should really be a tree depth of -infinity.

messages.subject: treedepth__ off by -1
messages.body_plain:
There's an off-by-one error in our tree depth reporting.
I just created an issue to fix it.

Here's the usual definition of depth

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_tree#Definitions_for_rooted_trees

according to which we have this:

      TREE             DEPTH   NODES      LEAPFROG STEPS
     theta1 :          0       2^0 = 1       0

     theta1...theta2   1       2^1 = 2       1

     theta1...theta4:  2       2^2 = 4       3

and what Stan is reporting as treedepth__ is really depth - 1.

The only note in the manual is that it's log2(# leapfrog steps).
In terms of leapfrog steps, what we currently report is this:

     log(# leapfrog steps + 1) - 1

I know it's a bit of backward incompatibility for commands, but I
think it'd be much easier to stick to the standard way of measuring
tree depth.

I created an issue for the next release with items to change the
code and doc.

- Bob

messages.subject: solved 2.0.0 efficiency issue; patch early this week
messages.subject_clean: solved 2.0.0 efficiency issue; patch early this week
messages.body_plain:
Daniel Lee and Michael Betancourt put in a heroic amount
of effort this weekend to solve the problem with 2.0.

Thank you from all of us!   And thanks to FHRB Toledo,
who submitted the model that sent us on this merry
bug chase.

I just confirmed the fix.  Timing and effective sample
sizes (including variation across chains) are now similar in
1.3 and 2.0.

Daniel and I will put together a 2.0.1 release as soon
as we can and it should be easy for Jiqiang to update RStan
and Allen to update PyStan (which we'll also be announcing
real soon).

The problem is isolated to the multivariate normal's gradient
calculation.  The multivariate normal was refactored for
speed in 2.0, but not tested well enough.

To validate the source of our issue, I just rolled back to the
1.3 definition of multivariate normal.  We should be able to fix
the root cause of 2.0's derivative error, at which point, 2.0
should be faster than 1.3 for this model.

The fact that HMC is just Metropolis with a fancy proposal
and the usual reject step meant that the bug didn't manifest itself
in the wrong answers, just in poorer proposals, which are much harder
to diagnose.

Michael and Daniel also fixed an issue in finite differences
introduced as part of 2.0, which allowed them to spot the bug
in the first place.

- Bob

Beyond the issue of insufficient testing, regression bugs like these should be easily git bisected:

  -- Write a script that returns a failure if the model doesn't complete in a reasonable amount of time
  -- git bisect start
  -- git bisect good v1.3.0
  -- git bisect bad
  -- git bisect run ./script.sh

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Possible bug(s) in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I don't think we can create a unit test until we
know where the problem is.

Maybe instrumenting the code to see if the method in which
its stuck percolates up.  The problem's most likely in one
of the custom derivative functions.

Otherwise, I'd just start taking out bits of the model.
But how often does it run into problems?

Yes, we pretty much have to allow NaN without exception if
we give users the power to do floating point arithmetic.
As soon as they do 0 / 0 it's game over.

Right now, we also have not added any error checking to
standard library calls, so log(-1) will cause the same
problem.  In and of itself, this should only cause a rejection.

- Bob

messages.subject: bug in gamma_q_vv_vari::chain (was: Re: Possible bug(s) in Stan?)
messages.subject_clean: bug in gamma_q_vv_vari::chain (was: Re: Possible bug(s) in Stan?)
messages.body_plain:
The infinite loop is in:

   gamma_q_vv_vari::chain()

Instruments picked it up in no time.

The offending loop appears to be this one:

   while (std::fabs(delta) > 1e-6) {
     ...
   }

We can't just assume iterative algorithms will terminate.
They need to count iterations of the loop and terminate after
some finite number of steps and throw a non-convergence error.

I'll track it down a bit more closely and create the issue and a branch
with a unit test that fails.  But I'm not even sure what this function
is, so I don't think I should be the one to fix it!

- Bob

messages.subject: Adept auto-dif lib
messages.body_plain:
An off-list request pointed me to a new auto-diff lib
that looks interesting:

   http://www.met.reading.ac.uk/clouds/adept/

There are links to papers and the software itself is C++
expression-template based and released under GPLv3.

We haven't gotten to expression templates, as we have instead
been focusing on doing the same sort of thing by hand for
operations we care about, like the matrix and probability functions.

But there's definitely the potential there to use them in the
usual way to accelerate operations.  Especially simple things like
addition that otherwise bloat the expression tree.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Adept auto-dif lib
messages.body_plain:
Nope -- I should take a look.  It's certainly possible
to code generate reverse-mode auto-diff --- it's what
the Fortran libs all did.  I believe the complications
come in through conditional structures (including loop
bounds), because you need to figure out the order of
traversal of the expression graph (now implicit in local
variables) in the reverse pass.

   if (a)
     x = 2 * x;
   else
     x = x / 2;

Now how do you propagate the derivative back?  You need
to code-generate both branches and then store the result
of the loop conditional somehow to decide whether to divide
or multiply by 2.

We also need higher-order auto-diff for a lot of
the things we're looking at doing near term, but we
all know that's not going to scale as the number of
parameters grow.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inv_wishart behavior
messages.body_plain:
Yeah, but that just means heavy tails which shouldn't be a problem for Stan.  Most of the marginals look like student distributions (with a relatively small FWHM and the occasionally large excursion) (and the correlations of the latent Ws with the log_posterior are all funnel like, which is pretty cool).

I think we just need to add init=0 (or init=0.1 if you want to have randomness) .  What seems to be happening is that a large random starts the chain way out in the tails where the trajectories drift with little gradient information to guide them to the typical set and you just get a long meandering random walk that never really converges.  The marginals have pretty small FWHMs so the inits have to be pretty tight, but tight inits seem to improve sampling significantly.

messages.subject: RStan + Mavericks install instructions
messages.body_plain:
I just verified by "upgrading" my own Macbook to Mavericks that the
instructions put together by Jiqiang and Avi Feller work as advertised.

I trimmed Avi's suggestion down to something a bit smaller and added
a note to the pre-requisites section of our basic instructions:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started

the content of which is:

-----------------------------------------------------------------
Special Steps for Xcode 5.0.1, R 3.0.2, and Mac OS X 10.9 (Mavericks)

To use the latest tools:

  * Mac OS X version 10.9 (aka Mavericks),
  * Xcode toolset version 5.0.1 including the latest command-line tools
    for Mavericks (now a separate download from Xcode), and
  * R version 3.0.2 (installed in the usual way from the precompiled
    binary .pkg file),

you need to create the file

   ~/.R/Makevars

with content

  CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++
  CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"

before proceeding.  Without the architecture and library link, the library will build but can't be linked to R.

Note that the compiler clang++ can be specified instead of g++ in the CXX definition.
----------------------------------------------------------------

I only tested with the latest R (3.0.2) and Xcode (5.0.1).  I
started by uninstalling the older Xcode and R versions and reinstalling,
but that shouldn't be necessary if you already have them installed
(including the command-line tools for Xcode, which are now a separate download).

Of course, you need to otherwise follow the usual instructions by uninstalling any
old versions of Stan first with remove.packages('rstan').

Let us know if you are still having problems after creating the above Makevars file.
If you are still having problems, please send us the versions of Mac OS X, Xcode and
R that you're using and let us know how you installed them.  Also, send the result
of running the following two commands from a terminal window:

    $ R CMD config CXX

    $ g++ -v

For me, after updating my Makevars file as above, they report

   $ R CMD config CXX
   g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++

and

   $ g++ -v
   Configured with: --prefix=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/usr --with-gxx-include-dir=/usr/include/c++/4.2.1
   Apple LLVM version 5.0 (clang-500.2.79) (based on LLVM 3.3svn)
   Target: x86_64-apple-darwin13.0.0
   Thread model: posix

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inv_wishart behavior
messages.body_plain:
> > The flexible adaptation branch has a proper warmup window so that should help.
>
> Meaning you can set it?

Yes, the init window, the adaptation window, and the termination window are all customizable.

> Can't we do something simpler to learn a bit about
> covariance early on, then be less agressive about
> step size adaptation?  (I know these things are much easier
> to say than tune!)

We should ease back on the stepsize initialization a bit but we need to finish some experiments
to validate that first.  But there's really not much you can do in only 20 iterations to learn the
variances better.

> I have looked, but often what's happening is that iteration 20 or
> so is about where the algorithm seems to have converged to the right
> region of the posterior.
>
> So is the covariance that was being used
> out in the tail out of whack so that when you get closer
> to convergence, the scale's all wrong?  If so, maybe tamping down
> the scale of the covariance matrix more strongly during warmup would
> help.

The biggest issue is that the covariance estimates are hugely overestimated because
they incorporate the huge swing in the warmup.  In the next adaptation window those
estimates would be wiped, but the chain isn't getting there fast enough.  This is what
the init window is meant to ameliorate.
